claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.

Integrating in-situ DIC tensile/fracture testing with an active-learning reduced-order mesoscale model will enable rapid and accurate prediction of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and phase boundaries in the hierarchical heterostructure mediate local stress concentrations and crack dynamics.
High-resolution real-time DIC can monitor microcrack evolution in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Feeding DIC crack-evolution data into an active-learning simulation will refine predictions of mechanical response.
Linking observed crack dynamics to the simulation will address the difficulty of predicting fracture toughness.
The reduced-order active-learning approach will reduce reliance on computationally intensive full-scale first-principles calculations.
Ab initio and molecular-dynamics methods are time-consuming and difficult to apply in high-throughput alloy-structure prediction.
CALPHAD modeling can require significant computational resources and can be limited by the absence of reliable HEA databases.
Machine-learning prediction accuracy is sensitive to the size and composition of the training dataset.
Prior stand-alone machine-learning models have lower efficiency and limited fracture-toughness accuracy for HfNbTiVAl10.
Quantitative fracture-toughness characterization can be difficult and common indentation-crack estimates can be unreliable.
The integrated method will predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness within approximately 10% of experimental values.
The integrated method will reduce computational demands by at least 70% relative to conventional first-principles and CALPHAD methods.
The method may become unreliable when the hierarchical heterostructure is not reproducible.
The method may become unreliable at strain rates, temperatures, or environmental conditions outside its calibration domain.
The method may become unreliable if phase transitions or other changes produce crack-propagation mechanisms absent from the simulation.
Model transferability to different loading rates or temperatures is uncertain.
Prediction errors exceeding 10% across a statistically significant blinded sample set would falsify the proposed accuracy claim.
